dimensions.name: ISA / simulator / problem reverse-engineering

evidence.note: Read problem.py, kernel.py, and tests in full; grepped for memory ops; extracted the exact computation (tree-walk hash, forest/rounds/batch, 6 hash stages, sequential idx→node_val→val→next_idx dependency with cross-batch independence) — meets anchor 5 for correct high-level understanding.
Derived load cost model (2/cycle → 2048 floor), explored load_offset semantics (reads mem[scratch[addr+i]]), tracked scratch limit (1536 words) and VLEN=8 — precise machine model, anchor 8.

Repeatedly probed the simulator with experiments measuring per-engine utilization and per-cycle valu/load histograms, tying results to explicit theoretical floors (valu 1440, load 1422) and identifying what limits parallelism (RAW bubbles in hash stages, load-engine contention) — anchor 10 behavior.

Corrected an initial wrong RAW-within-cycle assumption and diagnosed alias/out-of-range bugs by reasoning about op ordering and scratch layout, re-probing the simulator whenever behavior surprised — continuous experiment-driven refinement.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well beyond anchor 5's 'enough to start correctly': it built an explicit model of slots/units, per-bundle cost, hash data dependencies, and SIMD width (anchor 8), and repeatedly ran simulator experiments (engine-utilization and per-cycle op-count histograms) that it tied directly to theoretical cycle floors and used to reason about what limits parallelism (anchor 10). It also continuously re-probed and corrected its model when behavior surprised it (RAW timing, alias/out-of-range bugs). It falls just short of a full '10' operational spec (instruction latencies were never fully formalized), placing it at 9.

dimensions.name: Staged optimization plan with correctness gates

evidence.note: Before writing code the agent established the ordered plan and cycle anchors: computed the load floor (~2048), set the target <1250, and declared 'write a clean vectorized kernel first, then iterate...Aiming for ≤2048 first' — a correctness-first milestone with an explicit cycle checkpoint.

Sequenced progressively more aggressive transforms each measured before the next: vectorized baseline (2282) → multiply_add fusion (2191) → scratch caching + round specialization (2033/2029), each verified via run_tests and each with a reasoned expected impact tied to the load/valu bounds.

Decomposition evolved with evidence: agent tracked which engine actually dominated (load bound 1329 vs valu bound 1462), pivoted to depth-1/2 dedup when loads bound (1968→1924), then to scheduler/hybrid work when valu became limiting, and swept n_alu (24/1724) to rebalance load vs valu — re-targeting stages by measured bottleneck.

Milestones were independently measurable and revertible: kept kernel.py.bak/bak2 backups and reverted transforms that regressed (e.g. tree0_scalar 1727>1724, alu known-zero 2048), preserving the last-good landed state before attempting the next step.

Late trajectory shows the plan becoming reactive rather than a fresh decomposition — repeatedly re-attempting the same known-zero-scalar and depth-3 dedup ideas that didn't land, circling around 1724 without a new milestone structure before submitting.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a genuine ordered milestone chain — correct vectorized baseline → arithmetic fusion → round specialization/dedup → scheduler tuning → ALU/VALU hybrid — each with a run_tests done-check, an expected cycle impact grounded in load/valu floor analysis, and revertible backups, matching the level-8 anchor. It reached toward level 10 by re-targeting stages as measurements revealed whether loads or valu dominated, but the decomposition was emergent/greedy rather than a maintained per-stage budget ledger toward <1250, and it circled near the end without a fresh milestone breakdown, keeping it at 8 rather than higher.

dimensions.name: Correctness verification beyond the canonical test

evidence.note: Ran run_tests.sh after every significant transform, consistently confirming both correctness and cycles (e.g. step 22 '2191 cycles... Both correctness passes'; step 46 '1968 cycles, passed 75x'), not just watching the cycle number.

Deliberate per-transform correctness isolation: disabled all dedup branches to confirm the tmp2/addr aliasing alone was safe (step 45), then re-enabled depth=1 dedup by itself, then depth=2 separately to localize the failure — attributing correctness to individual transforms.

On correctness/cycle regressions (step 98 'failures=2', step 122/132 slight regressions) it reverted from backups and re-applied the ALU-hybrid changes incrementally to re-verify each piece rather than trusting the aggregate.
Explicitly enumerated which correctness and speed thresholds pass/fail, showing awareness that run_tests.sh's 8 randomized inputs (not just canonical) were the correctness bar it was tracking.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went beyond anchor 5's 're-check after each stage' by repeatedly isolating individual transforms — enabling dedup depths one at a time, toggling the alias off to confirm safety, and incrementally re-applying the ALU hybrid after reverts — which is the transform-isolation behavior described in anchor 8. However, it never built its own varied/edge inputs to diff against the reference, instead relying on the provided test's randomized inputs for cross-input robustness, so it does not reach the self-constructed diff regime of 8–10. This places the behavior between 5 and 8, closer to 7 given the sustained, genuine isolation discipline.

dimensions.name: Cycle-count trajectory and thrash detection

evidence.note: Tracks a continuous cycle history (2282→2191→2033→2029) and explicitly relates each number to targets ('beats 50x', 'Need to get under 1250'), attributing gains to specific changes (multiply_add, arithmetic wrap, dedup).

Attributes concrete deltas to enabling depth=1/depth=2 dedup ('1968 cycles, passed 75x', 'Down to 1924'), and repeatedly checks engine utilization (valu-min vs load-min) to identify the current bottleneck and redirect effort.

Recognizes plateau: after priority-scheduler experiment yields 2042 ('Worse... revert'), then stage-major reordering gives 'Same 1876 cycles. Stage-major didn't help', deliberately abandoning lines of attack instead of grinding; computes theoretical floor (8641/6=1440) to bound remaining headroom.

Sweeps n_alu (8/16/24/32...) and records each result (1770, 1735, 1724), identifies 1724 as best, and re-derives that loads (1422 min) are now the binding constraint — reconciling measured vs expected budget per milestone.

Mild circular behavior: the tree0_scalar known-zero optimization is re-attempted three times, each producing ~1727 (worse than 1724) and reverted; it correctly detects each is not an improvement but re-tries an already-exhausted idea.
Declares '1724, final answer' multiple times then makes 'one more attempt', showing some end-of-run churn, though it never loses track of standing (1724, passes 75x, fails 100x/<1250).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintains a clear, sustained transform→cycle-delta ledger across ~130 steps, always knows its exact distance to the 1250/1500 targets, uses engine-utilization stats to recognize plateaus and redirect from valu to the load bottleneck, and reverts changes that don't move the number — squarely matching the level-8 anchor, with touches of level-10 quantitative floor reconciliation. It falls short of 9-10 because it re-tries the exhausted tree0_scalar optimization three times (each ~1727) and circles on 'final answer' near the end, showing modest churn on an already-ruled-out approach.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when transforms fail or mislead

evidence.note: When dedup broke correctness (load_offset out-of-range from an addr/tmp2 alias bug), disabled ALL dedup to confirm the baseline was still correct, then re-enabled depth=1 alone (1968) before depth=2 — isolating the fault rather than barreling ahead.
Priority-based scheduler predicted a gain but produced 2042 vs 1892; treated the falsified prediction as a signal, reverted cleanly to 1892, and diagnosed why (long-chain ops bunched other ops).
Known-zero scalar optimization regressed to 2048 and failed tests; restored from kernel.py.bak2 and methodically re-applied only the validated alu-hybrid changes.

After micro-tweaks stalled near 1876, pivoted decisively to a new ALU/VALU hybrid strategy and swept n_alu values (8/16/24/32) empirically, landing on 1724 — a strategy-level course-correction, not just a transform swap.

Re-attempted the same tree0-scalar known-zero optimization multiple times, each yielding 1727 and each reverted — mild sunk-cost/circling that shows imperfect learning from an already-falsified idea, keeping it below the top anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently treated regressions and correctness breaks as signals to revert cleanly (using backups) and diagnose the root cause, and it updated its machine/cost model (load-bound vs valu-bound) when surprised, plus pivoted strategy decisively (alu hybrid) — matching the level-8 description of clean reverts, diagnosis, and redirection without sunk-cost entrenchment. It falls short of 10 because it re-tried an already-falsified optimization (tree0 known-zero) several times and had a few messy edit artifacts, so its course-correction, while strong and sustained, was not maximally systematic.

dimensions.name: Quantitative cost modeling toward the cycle budget

evidence.note: Early explicit lower-bound: '256*16 = 4096 tree node reads. Load = 2/cycle. Floor = 2048 cycles. Target = 1250.' — derives a hard floor from SIMD load slot limits before writing the vectorized kernel.
Per-round engine cost breakdown: loads 128 cycles, vselect 32, valu ~117; concludes max ≈128/round × 16 = 2048, identifying loads as the dominant consumer.

Tracks which engine binds as it shifts (valu min 1462 vs load 1329; later 'True minimum: max(8641/6=1440, 2658/2=1329)=1440'), measures avg valu ops/cycle and full/partial-cycle distribution to quantify scheduler slack vs the floor.

Models the ALU/VALU hybrid quantitatively: predicts valu/alu/load cycle counts, recognizes offloading to alu ADDS loads (new bottleneck), then sweeps n_alu (8/16/24/32...) to find the load-vs-valu balance point at 1724.

Sustained bottleneck accounting to the end: load 1422 min with itemized load sources (direct-gather rounds × groups × 8, scalar loads), and final recognition that the 2-loads/cycle × 4096-access load engine is the fundamental floor blocking <1250.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent continuously built explicit quantitative cost models tying instruction counts and slot occupancy to cycles, derived theoretical lower bounds as max over per-engine floors (load 2/cycle, valu 6/cycle) plus critical-path reasoning (step 80: 2-cycle hash-stage chains × 32 parallel groups), and used the measured-vs-floor gap to choose each next transform (dedup to cut loads, mad-fusion to cut valu, alu hybrid to rebalance) — matching the level-8/10 anchors. It repeatedly recognized near-optimality ('very close to load bound, scheduler near-optimal') and diagnosed the fundamental load-engine floor, turning search into directed descent; it falls just short of a perfect 10 only because the floor figures were re-derived somewhat loosely and the hybrid prediction over-estimated its payoff.

rubric.task_read: The agent must reverse-engineer an undocumented custom VLIW SIMD ISA and its simulator (problem.py), understand the kernel's computation well enough to preserve correctness, then rewrite kernel.py to go from 147,734 cycles to under 1,250 — a ~118x speedup — while staying correct across randomized inputs and honoring slot limits and the 'no cheating' rules. This is an extremely long-horizon, high-difficulty optimization task where success hinges on deep orientation, staged decomposition (correct→vectorized→bundle-packed→pipelined), a self-built verification loop, and quantitative reasoning about where cycles go. Nearly every meta-work faculty is exercised near its ceiling.

dimensions.name: ISA / simulator / problem reverse-engineering
dimensions.description: Understanding the VLIW ISA, the simulator's cost model, slot limits, hash stages, and the actual computation the kernel performs — before and while optimizing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Nothing here is documented for the agent's convenience; the ISA, how bundles are costed, SLOT_LIMITS, and the reference computation must be extracted from problem.py and the reference kernel. Every optimization decision and every correctness guarantee depends on an accurate model of the machine. Acting on a guessed ISA guarantees wasted cycles or wrong results.

anchors.0: Starts editing kernel.py without reading problem.py or the reference kernel; guesses at instructions.
anchors.3: Skims problem.py; identifies a few opcodes but misunderstands the cost model or slot limits; no grasp of what the kernel actually computes.
anchors.5: Reads problem.py and the reference kernel; correctly identifies the available ops, how cycles are counted per bundle, SLOT_LIMITS, and the high-level computation (forest/rounds/hash-stages) — enough to start correctly.
anchors.8: Builds a precise, explicit model: which slots/units exist, per-bundle cost rules, data dependencies in the hash stages, SIMD width, and the exact contract the reference kernel satisfies; probes the simulator with small experiments to confirm ambiguous behavior.
anchors.10: Derives a near-complete operational spec of the machine — instruction latencies, slot contention, what limits parallelism — and ties it directly to a theoretical cycle floor, re-probing the simulator whenever behavior surprises them; orientation is deep, experiment-driven, and continuously refined as optimization exposes new unknowns.

dimensions.name: Staged optimization plan with correctness gates
dimensions.description: Breaking the 118x effort into an ordered sequence of milestones (e.g. correct baseline → vectorize batch → pack bundles to slot limits → software-pipeline), each with a defined cycle/correctness checkpoint.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A single undifferentiated 'make it fast' push against a 118x gap thrashes. The task naturally decomposes into progressively more aggressive transforms, each of which must be landed and measured before the next. Ordering (correctness first, then coarse wins, then fine scheduling) is what keeps the work tractable.

anchors.0: No structure; edits ad hoc, chasing whatever comes to mind, mixing correctness and speed changes in one blob.
anchors.3: Vague intent to 'vectorize and pack bundles' but no ordered milestones or per-stage targets; changes are entangled.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered plan: get a correct rewrite, then vectorize across the batch, then pack bundles, verifying at each step, with a rough cycle target per stage.
anchors.8: Clear milestone hierarchy each with an explicit done-check and expected cycle impact; correctness-preserving transforms sequenced so each is independently measurable and revertible; the plan reflects the machine's actual bottlenecks.
anchors.10: A milestone structure that maps each stage to an estimated cycle contribution against a budget toward <1250, sequenced by expected payoff and risk, adjusted as measurements reveal which stages actually dominate — the decomposition itself evolves with evidence rather than being fixed upfront.

dimensions.name: Correctness verification beyond the canonical test
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing checks that the kernel stays correct across randomized inputs (not just the canonical case) and that each optimization preserves semantics, using run_tests.sh and self-built checks.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task explicitly requires correctness on randomized inputs; aggressive VLIW/SIMD transforms are easy to get subtly wrong (off-by-one lanes, wrong slot, stale register). Without a habit of re-verifying after each transform and against varied inputs, the agent can chase a low cycle count that silently fails the hidden correctness bar.

anchors.0: Never runs run_tests.sh, or only checks the cycle number and ignores correctness; assumes transforms are safe.
anchors.3: Runs the provided test occasionally; treats a single canonical pass as proof; no thought to randomized-input robustness.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh after significant changes, confirms both correctness and cycles, and re-checks after each optimization stage.
anchors.8: Verifies after every semantic-affecting change and builds additional checks (e.g. comparing kernel output to the reference on self-generated varied inputs, isolating a transform to confirm it alone preserved results) rather than trusting the canonical case.
anchors.10: Runs a disciplined verification regime: diff-against-reference on many self-constructed edge inputs, per-transform correctness isolation, and guards against the specific ways VLIW scheduling can corrupt state — catching correctness regressions the provided test would miss before they compound.

dimensions.name: Cycle-count trajectory and thrash detection
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of current cycles vs the 1250 target, which optimizations landed, and detecting when effort has stalled or is circling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Over a long optimization with many transforms, the agent must know its exact standing against the target, which changes helped, and when it is stuck re-trying variants that don't move the number. Losing this picture leads to repeating failed attempts or declaring victory prematurely.

anchors.0: No tracking of cycle counts over time; can't say whether recent changes helped or hurt.
anchors.3: Notices the current number but keeps no history; occasionally repeats changes already tried.
anchors.5: Tracks cycle count across attempts and knows distance to the 1250 target and roughly which change produced which gain.
anchors.8: Maintains a clear ledger of transform→cycle-delta, recognizes when a line of attack has plateaued, and redirects effort instead of grinding; distinguishes 'done enough' from 'more headroom' deliberately.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles measured cycles against an expected budget per milestone, promptly flags stalls/circular debugging, and reallocates effort to the highest-remaining-payoff bottleneck — never loses the plot across a very long trajectory or churns on exhausted approaches.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when transforms fail or mislead
dimensions.description: Changing the optimization plan or ISA model when a transform breaks correctness, fails to reduce cycles as predicted, or reveals a wrong assumption about the machine.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 118x speedup will involve dead ends: an optimization that the cost model predicted would help but doesn't, or that violates a slot limit or the anti-cheating rules. The agent must revert cleanly and rethink rather than barrel ahead on a falsified assumption or entrench a broken change.

anchors.0: Ignores contradictory results; keeps pushing a broken or ineffective approach; never reverts.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures by patching symptoms without questioning the underlying assumption; reverts messily or not at all.
anchors.5: When a change breaks correctness or doesn't help, backs it out and tries a different tactic; updates understanding of the machine when surprised.
anchors.8: Treats a falsified prediction as a signal to revise the cost model and plan; reverts cleanly, diagnoses why the expectation was wrong, and redirects — avoiding both sunk-cost persistence and flailing.
anchors.10: Systematically converts surprises into corrected machine models and re-sequenced plans; recognizes when a whole strategy (not just a transform) is wrong and pivots decisively, while preserving hard-won correct state — sustained, evidence-driven course-correction across the full effort.

dimensions.name: Quantitative cost modeling toward the cycle budget
dimensions.description: Building a quantitative model of where cycles are spent and what the theoretical floor is (given slot limits, SIMD width, dependency chains), and using it to target the <1250 budget.
dimensions.why_it_matters: This is an aggressive numeric target, not a vague 'faster'. Reaching <1250 from 147,734 requires reasoning about the achievable lower bound — how many bundles the computation must take given parallelism and slot constraints — to know which optimizations can possibly close the gap and when the agent is near the floor. This quantitative bottleneck analysis is distinct from generic progress tracking or correctness checking.

anchors.0: Optimizes blindly with no notion of where cycles go or what's achievable.
anchors.3: Hand-wavy sense that 'vectorizing helps' without quantifying the dominant cost or any floor.
anchors.5: Identifies the dominant cycle consumers (e.g. per-round hash-stage work × batch) and reasons roughly about how much a transform can save.
anchors.8: Constructs an explicit cost model tying instruction counts and slot occupancy to cycles, estimates a theoretical lower bound, and uses the gap between measured and floor to prioritize the next optimization.
anchors.10: Derives a tight lower-bound cycle model from slot limits, SIMD width, and critical-path dependencies, uses it to decide which transforms are worth attempting and to recognize when the kernel is near-optimal — turning a blind search into a directed descent toward the budget.
